summary:
Scotland stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The daily consequence for a trans visitor in Scotland is that facilities designated by biological sex are the ones to be used, with organisations instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The competing arguments were aired in the same court on 5 February 2026, when it was argued that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard and For Women Scotland pressed its challenge to the policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

Searching and strip-searching policy follows the same principle. On 17 April 2025 British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, adopting an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth; the prior policy had permitted trans women staff to intimately search women holding a gender recognition certificate, and Sex Matters welcomed the change. On 25 June 2025 Police Scotland published interim guidance under which searches in custody and stop-and-search involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, with efforts made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request where lived gender differs.

Gender recognition documents carry their own consequences. In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the ground that those jurisdictions allowed people to transition too easily; people from those locations must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. The Women and Equalities Minister, Kemi Badenoch, called the changes long overdue, while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Within the UK, a certificate will not be issued unless the applicant's spouse consents; where the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated, and transgender people seeking a certificate have historically been required to divorce or annul first.

Access to gender-affirming care is restricted for minors. NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, a suspension renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and due to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. The Cass Review of April 2024 also led NHS England to close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. Bell v Tavistock (December 2020) had found that children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers; that judgment was overturned on appeal in September 2021.

Restrictions reach schools and sport. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a gender recognition certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams. Transgender youth are otherwise covered by the Equality Act 2010. On 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Scotland operates its own hate-crime machinery, and charges carrying a transgender-identity aggravation are rising. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported in Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26, published 30 June 2026, that 7,115 hate-crime charges were brought in 2025-26, up 17 per cent on 2024-25 and the highest total since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, a rise of 21 per cent from 86 and the highest level recorded since the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021 took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. A trans visitor therefore enters a jurisdiction where trans-motivated offences are actively charged under a dedicated statutory aggravator, at a level the prosecuting service describes as the highest since the provision began.
tangentialFactors:
Hate-crime volume in Scotland is concentrated in larger cities and dominated by racial aggravation, which situates the transgender figures within a broader pattern. Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25, with the highest rates per 10,000 residents in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each; 62 per cent carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator. That report, published by the Scottish Government on 17 February 2026, was the first annual publication under the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021.

Recorded hate crimes and prosecuted hate-crime charges are counted on different bases and for different years, so the 8,538 recorded offences for 2024-25 and the 7,115 charges for 2025-26 are not directly comparable, though both trend upward and both show the 2021 Act in active use.

The trajectory of transgender-identity charges is the sharpest signal in the data: 104 charges in 2025-26 against 86 the previous year, an increase of 21 per cent in a single year, against a general hate-crime charge total that rose 17 per cent. External scrutiny is running alongside the domestic policy direction, with UN human rights experts warning on 18 August 2026 that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Residents of Scotland are covered by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, which provides a specific transgender-identity aggravation; the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service prosecutes under it, and the 2025-26 figures mark the highest level of such charges since the Act commenced. Residents also report and record hate crime through Police Scotland, whose recorded figures for 2024-25 form the first annual Scottish Government report under the Act.

For people in custody, the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance no longer stands: the Outer House of the Court of Session held it unlawful on 19 June 2026, so sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis, and any continued placement of trans prisoners by gender identity requires a fresh lawful footing. Searches in police custody and stop-and-search follow Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025, which ties searches involving removal of more than outer clothing to biological sex while providing an officer of the person's lived gender on request where that differs.

Residents seeking to change legal gender must obtain a UK gender recognition certificate, and a certificate will not be issued without spousal consent, failing which the marriage must be terminated. Certificates issued by 50 named countries and U.S. states are no longer recognised for this purpose, so residents holding such a document must apply afresh under British law. Transgender residents covered by the Equality Act 2010 retain statutory protection, and youth provision runs through schools and sports bodies applying single-sex rules, including the Girls' Day School Trust and the RFU and RFL policies for under-12s.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state whether the equality watchdog's single-sex spaces code and the codes and guidance issued at UK level are applied in Scotland by a separate Scottish body or by the same one, and no Scottish-specific compliance mechanism for the code is sourced here.

The care restrictions cited are NHS England measures: the March 2024 puberty-blocker pause, its December 2024 renewal and 2027 review date, the April 2025 report of no new hormone prescriptions to minors, the closure of the Tavistock GIDS and the opening of two of eight regional centres. Whether NHS Scotland applies identical restrictions, and what provision exists in Scotland for minors and adults, remains unresolved on this inventory.

The 104 transgender-identity charges reported for 2025-26 are charges, not convictions; no conviction, sentencing or case-outcome data for trans-motivated offences in Scotland is sourced, nor is any breakdown of those charges by location, victim profile or alleged conduct. The comparison between the 8,538 recorded hate crimes of 2024-25 and the 7,115 charges of 2025-26 is left unresolved here because the two series cover different years and different stages of the process.

No Scotland-specific data is sourced on whether trans visitors have been refused accommodation, entry to facilities or services under the August 2026 single-sex spaces code, and no reported enforcement action against an organisation under that code is available in this inventory.
